newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN STRIKE BITES IN KWAZULU-NATAL PROVINCE.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN STRIKE BITES IN KWAZULU-NATAL PROVINCE.

text.p: Employers reported a strong response in KwaZulu-Natal province on Tuesday to the South African labour federation Cosatu's second day of protest action against the Basic Conditions of Employment Bill.

Cosatu, the 1.9 million-member Congress of South African Trade Unions, has scheduled four days of regional strikes ending on Thursday to press for tougher bottom-line employment conditions in a bill due to go to parliament on September 15.
A spokesman for the Durban Chamber of Commerce and Industry said early on Tuesday the strike call seemed to be effective, but that figures were not immediately available.
"It looks like the strike is fairly well supported at this stage," John Bryce told Reuters.
Durban harbour was affected by the stayaway with no breakbulk cargo being handled, a Portnet spokeswoman said.
"The container services are 67 percent operational. Road transport services have been affected, but I don't have figures," said Portnet spokeswoman Yvonne de Kock.
Business and labour representatives told national radio on Tuesday there was no sign of an imminent breakthrough in their dispute over minimum terms proposed by Labour Minister Tito Mboweni.

Labour wants a commitment in the bill to reduce the maximum working week to 40 hours within five years, but business is unwilling to go beyond the proposed reduction 45 hours. They are also in dispute over maternity leave and overtime pay proposals.
A spokeswoman for Durban Metro train service said trains were running at about 60 percent of usual levels.
"We have not had any major problems reported so far. About a third of our guards are out on strike, but all the train drivers have pitched up to work," Claudia Williams said.
Police said an incident of intimidation was reported near the black township of Umlazi near Durban where a bus carrying workers was stoned. No injuries were reported.
Employer federations reported on Monday that about 70 percent of the total workforce had stayed away in the Eastern Cape province, where Cosatu launched its campaign.
Cosatu said in a statement about 95 percent of its members backed the strike in the southcoast region around Port Elizabeth and East London.

Auke Keyser, president of the Nelspruit District Chamber of Commerce and Industry, said there was a strong response from workers at bigger companies in eastern Mpumalanga on Tuesday, but that smaller employers were reported near full turn-outs.
Marches by Cosatu in the major centres of Durban and Pietermaritzburg are expected for Tuesday afternoon.
